identityCheck: The text title 'Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' (Stevens et al., International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2025) matches the filename.

paper.citation: Stevens CJ, Borg D, Brade C, Carter S, Filingeri D, Lee J, Lim L, Mündel T, Taylor L, Tyler CJ. Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2025 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis pooled 63 controlled trials (618 participants, 86.6% male, almost all crossover) testing head, face or neck cooling on physical or cognitive performance. Cooling reduced skin temperature at the target site and improved thermal sensation and comfort. Pooled effects on exercise performance were inconclusive, no harmful performance effects were found, and cognitive outcomes could not be pooled.
paper.tldr: Head, face and neck cooling improves thermal comfort and sensation during exercise and showed no harm to performance, but its effect on performance itself is inconclusive, so athletes should trial strategies to find what works for them.
paper.methods: The authors searched six databases and followed PRISMA guidance, with two reviewers screening studies and RoB 2 risk-of-bias assessment. Effects were pooled with a three-level meta-analysis using standardized mean differences for exercise tests and mean differences for physiological outcomes, with moderator and small-study bias checks.
paper.findings: Self-paced exercise tests gave a pooled SMD of 0.24 (95% CI -0.12 to 0.61) and fixed-intensity tests gave 0.35 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.61); the authors describe both as inconclusive and not harmful, although the fixed-intensity interval as reported excludes zero. Cooling lowered target-site skin temperature (MD -3.92 C) and improved thermal sensation and comfort, while heart rate was unchanged and core and mean skin temperature changes were small. Only three adverse event reports occurred across the 63 studies.
paper.limitations: Median sample size was 9, so most studies were underpowered, and 61 of 63 studies had some concerns on risk of bias. Participants were predominantly male (13.4% female) and spinal cord injury participants were 2.1%, while cognitive outcomes could not be meta-analysed because of inconsistent tests. Several studies used custom-made devices in controlled laboratory conditions.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes exposed to heat can trial head, face and neck cooling such as phase-change neck collars, face water spraying, cooling caps and iced towels, checking each strategy against sport rules. The review does not identify one superior method, and frozen gel packs on the forehead and eyes were poorly tolerated. Physiological monitoring is advised because perceived strain may not reflect true strain.
paper.athleteDev: Staff can recommend head, face and neck cooling during heat-exposed training or competition to improve thermal comfort and sensation, since no harmful performance effects were found. The performance benefit itself remains inconclusive, so cooling strategies should be trialled in training before use in competition.
paper.rtp: The review concerns cooling during exercise in healthy or trained people and does not address injury or return to sport. Its adverse-event data come from short heat-exposure trials and should not be used to guide clearance after heat illness or injury.
